ἀνθυποφέρῃ πρὸς ταῦτα, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι μὴ γενέσθαι ἃ τοιάδε ἔσεσθαι
προεγίνωσκεν ὁ θεός· φήσομεν ὅτι δυνατὸν μὲν μὴ γενέσθαι· οὐχὶ δέ, εἰ δυνατὸν μὴ
γενέσθαι, ἀνάγκη μὴ γενέσθαι ἢ γενέσθαι· καὶ γίνεται οὐ πάντως ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἀλλὰ
δυνατοῦ ὄντος καὶ τοῦ αὐτὰ μὴ γενέσθαι. τῆς δὲ λογικῆς ἔχεται ἐντρεχείας τε καὶ
θεωρίας ὁ περὶ τῶν δυνατῶν τόπος, ἵνα ὁ σμήξας ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ὄμμα τῆς ψυχῆς δυνηθῇ
τῇ λεπτότητι τῶν ἀποδείξεων παρακολουθήσας κατανοῆσαι, πῶς καὶ μέχρι τῶν
τυχόντων οὐκ ἐμποδίζεται τὸ εἶναί τι εἰς πολλὰ δυνατόν, ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν πολλῶν ὄντος
τοῦ ἐσομένου, καὶ οὐ κατὰ ἀνάγκην ἐσομένου· προεγνω σμένου τε οὑτωσί, ὅτι ἔσται
μὲν οὐκ ἐξ ἀνάγκης δὲ ἔσται, ἀλλ' ἐνδεχομένου τυγχάνοντος τοῦ μὴ γενέσθαι ἔσται
τὸ οὐ στοχαστικῶς εἰρημένον ἀλλ' ἀληθῶς προεγνωσμένον. μὴ νομιζέτω δέ τις ἡμᾶς
τὸ κατὰ πρόθε ιν σεσιωπηκέναι ὡς θλίβον ἡμῶν τὸν λόγον· ἐπεί φησιν ὁ Παῦλος
οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ι τὸν θεὸν πάντα υνεργεῖ εἰ ἀγαθόν, τοῖ κατὰ πρόθε ιν
κλητοῖ οὖ ιν. ἀλλὰ προσεχέτω ὅτι τοῦ κατὰ πρόθεσιν εἶναι κλητοὺς τὴν αἰτίαν καὶ ὁ
ἀπόστολος ἀποδέδωκεν εὐθέως, εἰπὼν ὅτι οὓ προέγνω, καὶ προώρι εν υμμόρφου
τῆ εἰκόνο τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ. καὶ τίνα γε μᾶλλον ἐχρῆν ἐγκαταχωρισθῆναι εἰς τὴν
δικαιοῦσαν κλῆσιν τῇ προθέσει τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας αὐτόν; πάνυ δὲ τὴν ἐκ
τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν αἰτίαν παρίστησι τῆς προθέσεως καὶ τῆς προγνώσεως τὸ οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι
τοῖ ἀγαπῶ ι τὸν θεὸν πάντα υνεργεῖ εἰ ἀγαθόν. σχεδὸν γὰρ εἶπεν ὅτι πάντα
συνεργοῦντα εἰς ἀγαθὸν διὰ τοῦτο συνεργεῖ, ἐπεὶ ἄξιοί εἰσι συνεργίας οἱ ἀγαπῶντες
τὸν θεόν. ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἐρωτήσωμεν τοὺς τὰ ἐναντία λέγοντας, καὶ ἀποκρινάσθωσαν
ἡμῖν πρὸς ταῦτα. ἔστω καθ' ὑπόθεσιν εἶναί τινα ἐφ' ἡμῖν· καὶ τοῦτο ἐροῦμεν αὐτοῖς
ἀναιροῦσι τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, ἕως ἐκ τῆς διδομένης ὑποθέσεως ἐλεγχθῇ αὐτῶν ὁ λόγος οὐχ
ὑγιὴς ὤν. ὄντος δὴ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, ἆρα ὁ θεὸς ἐπιβαλὼν τῷ εἱρμῷ τῶν ἐσομένων
προγνώσεται τὰ πραχθησόμενα ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἐχόντων τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, ἢ
οὐ προγνώσεται; τὸ μὲν οὖν λέγειν οὐ προγνώσεται, ἀγνοοῦντός ἐστι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι
νοῦν καὶ τὴν μεγαλωσύνην τοῦ θεοῦ. εἰ δὲ δώσουσιν ὅτι προγνώσεται, πάλιν
ἐρωτήσωμεν αὐτούς, ἆρα τὸ ἐγνωκέναι αὐτὸν αἴτιόν ἐστι τοῦ ἔσεσθαι τὰ ἐσόμενα,
διδομένου τοῦ εἶναι τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν; ἢ ἐπεὶ ἔσται προέγνω, καὶ οὐδαμῶς ἐστὶν αἰτία
αὐτοῦ ἡ πρόγνωσις τῶν ἐσομένων ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ἑκάστῳ; δυνατὸν οὖν ἦν τῶνδέ
τινων ἀπαντησάντων μὴ τόδε ἀλλὰ τόδε ἐνεργῆσαι τὸν δημιουργηθέντα
αὐτεξούσιον. τούτων οὖν καὶ τοιούτων ἂν λεχθησομένων, σώζεται καὶ τὸ εὖγε,

pass_a_gloss: If someone objects that these things could not have happened, we say it is possible they did not happen, but it does not follow that if something could not have happened, it must either happen or not happen; things occur not always by necessity, but also as possibilities, including the possibility that they might not happen. The discussion of possible things involves both logical reasoning and contemplation, so that one who examines their own mental eye may follow the subtlety of proofs and understand how even chance events do not prevent something from being possible in many ways, one of many possibilities being actual, not by necessity. God foreknew that things would happen not by necessity but as contingent possibilities, and the statement that they would happen is not conjectural but truly foreknown. Let no one think we have been silent about predestination as burdensome, for Paul says we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to purpose. But consider that the apostle immediately assigned the cause of those called according to purpose: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Who then should be assigned to the righteous calling by God’s purpose more than those who love him? Indeed, he makes evident the cause from us in purpose and foreknowledge: we know that all things work together for good for those who love God. For he nearly said that all things working together for good do so because those who love God are worthy of cooperation. At the same time, let us question those who speak oppositely and demand they answer us. Suppose hypothetically that something depends on us; we will tell them that they deny what depends on us until their argument is refuted by the given hypothesis as unsound. Given that something depends on us, does God, by imposing the order of future events, foreknow what will happen from what depends on us for each who has such dependence, or does he not? To say he does not foreknow is to ignore the universal mind and greatness of God. But if they say he does foreknow, let us ask: is his foreknowledge the cause of what will happen, given that what depends on us exists? Or, since he foreknew, is foreknowledge not at all the cause of what depends on us? It was possible for some of these people, having answered otherwise, to have acted differently, and the created self-determining being could have done otherwise. In such discussions, the saying 'Well done, good and faithful servant' is preserved, as well as 'You have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord.' Also preserved is the reasonable saying of the wicked and slothful servant: 'You ought to have put my money to the exchangers.' Only the rightly spoken words will be preserved: to those on the right, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' because I was hungry and you gave me food, and what follows; but to those on the left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,' because I was hungry and you gave me no food, nor what follows. Moreover, even if one were set apart for the gospel of God from the womb and had necessity laid upon them, how could they consistently speak of subduing their body and leading into slavery, if they had not yet been proclaimed by others as unapproved, and the woe would be theirs if they did not evangelize? Clearly, from these things it is shown that if they had not subdued their body and led into slavery, it would have been possible for them to be declared unapproved by others, and it was possible for woe to happen to them if they did not evangelize. Perhaps God both set them apart from the womb and for the gospel of God, together with seeing the cause of the just separation: that they would subdue their body and lead into slavery, being cautious lest they themselves, while proclaiming, become unapproved; and knowing that woe would happen to them if they did not evangelize, they did not remain silent out of fear of God regarding the woe, but evangelized. And these things were seen by the one who set them apart from the womb of their mother and the one who set them apart for their own gospel: that there would be labors, imprisonments, beatings beyond measure, frequent deaths; by the Jews five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned; and these things will happen to them.
pass_b_english: If someone insists these events could not have taken place, we respond that they might not have occurred, but it does not follow that if something is incapable of happening, it must either happen or fail to happen; events unfold not solely by necessity, but also as contingent possibilities, including the possibility of non-occurrence. The examination of what is possible engages both logical analysis and reflective insight, enabling one who turns inward to perceive the subtlety of arguments and grasp how even fortuitous occurrences do not obstruct the potential for something to be actual in multiple ways—one of many possibilities becoming real, not by compulsion. God foreknew that events would unfold not through necessity but as free possibilities, and the declaration that they would occur is not speculative guesswork but genuine foreknowledge. Let no one suppose we have remained silent on predestination as if it were a heavy burden, for Paul affirms we know that all things cooperate for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. Yet observe how the apostle immediately identifies the ground of this calling: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be shaped into the likeness of his Son. Who, then, is more fitting for the righteous vocation grounded in God’s purpose than those who love him? Indeed, he makes clear the source of this calling lies within us—our purpose and foreknowledge: we know that all things work together for good for those who love God. For he nearly said that such cooperation occurs because those who love God are worthy partners in the good. At the same time, let us challenge those who speak contrary views and demand they answer us. Assume hypothetically that something depends on us; we will tell them they reject what depends on us until their argument collapses under the weight of the given hypothesis as unsound. Given that something depends on us, does God, by ordaining the sequence of future events, foreknow what will arise from what depends on us in each case where such dependence exists, or does he not? To claim he does not foreknow is to overlook the universal intellect and grandeur of God. But if they affirm he does foreknow, let us ask: is his foreknowledge the cause of what will come to pass, given that what depends on us exists? Or, since he foreknew, is foreknowledge entirely irrelevant as a cause of what depends on us? It was possible for some of these individuals, having answered otherwise, to have acted differently, and the self-determining creature brought into being could have chosen otherwise. In such discourses, the words 'Well done, good and faithful servant' are preserved, as well as 'You have been faithful over little; I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord.' Likewise preserved is the reasonable utterance of the wicked and slothful servant: 'You ought to have put my money to the exchangers.' Moreover, even if one were set apart for the gospel of God from the womb and had necessity imposed upon them, how could they consistently speak of subduing their body and leading into slavery if they had not yet been declared unapproved by others, and the woe would be theirs if they did not evangelize? Clearly, from this it follows that if they had not subdued their body and led into slavery, it would have been possible for them to be declared unapproved by others, and it was possible for woe to befall them had they not evangelized. Perhaps God both set them apart from the womb and for the gospel of God, together with perceiving the cause of the just separation: that they would subdue their body and lead into slavery, wary lest they themselves, while proclaiming, become unapproved; and knowing that woe would come upon them if they did not evangelize, they did not remain silent out of fear of God regarding the woe, but evangelized. choices.issue: The relationship between divine foreknowledge and human freedom
choices.choice: God's foreknowledge does not cause future events but simply knows them as they arise from contingent human actions, preserving genuine self-determination.

choices.issue: The basis of predestination and calling
choices.choice: Those who love God are predestined not because of merit alone, but because God foreknew their responsive love and thus conformed them to Christ's image as part of his purpose.
